title: Bēowulf
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 55–58, lines 1473–1556 (fitt XXII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t: Bēowulf maþelode, bearn Ecgþēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: The house rendering of the speech formula, as at 1383: ‘maþelode’ is the past of ‘maþelian’, the verb that opens a formal speech, and ‘bearn Ecgþēowes’ is ‘child of Ecgtheow’, ‘bearn’ nominative in apposition to the name and ‘Ecgþēowes’ genitive. The colon opens Beowulf’s last speech before he enters the water.

sentences.t:
‘Geþenc nū, se mǣra maga Healfdenes,
snottra fengel, nū ic eom sīðes fūs,
goldwine gumena, hwæt wit geō sprǣcon,
sentences.l: ‘Consider now, you famous kinsman of Healfdene, wise prince, now that I am eager for the journey, gold-friend of men, what we two spoke formerly,
sentences.i: ‘Remember now, famous son of Healfdene, wise prince, gold-friend of men, now that I am ready for the journey, what we two said before,
sentences.n: ‘Geþenc’ is the imperative singular of ‘geþencan’, ‘think of, bear in mind’, and its object is the clause ‘hwæt wit geō sprǣcon’, ‘what we two once said’, where ‘wit’ is the dual pronoun, ‘we two’. ‘se mǣra maga Healfdenes’ is a vocative, ‘maga’ ‘son, kinsman’ (Hrothgar). ‘fūs’ with the genitive ‘sīðes’ is ‘eager for the journey’. ‘snottra fengel’ (‘wise prince’) and ‘goldwine gumena’ (‘gold-friend of men’, a lord who gives gold) are two more vocatives, the second a kenning for a generous king. The opening quotation mark is Klaeber’s, as printed in ‘t’.

sentences.t:
gif ic æt þearfe þīnre scolde
aldre linnan, þæt ðū mē ā wǣre
forðgewitenum on fæder stǣle.
sentences.l: if I at your need should lose my life, that you to me, departed, be ever in a father’s stead.
sentences.i: if I should lose my life in your need, that you would always be to me, once I am gone, as a father.
sentences.n: ‘gif ic … scolde aldre linnan’ is a conditional with ‘sculan’ in the past subjunctive, ‘if I should’; ‘linnan’ ‘cease, be deprived of’ takes the dative ‘aldre’, so ‘lose my life’. ‘æt þearfe þīnre’ is ‘at your need’, ‘þearfe’ a feminine dative with ‘þīnre’, the dative feminine of ‘þīn’, agreeing with it. The ‘þæt’ clause says what he asks of Hrothgar: ‘wǣre’ is subjunctive, and ‘forðgewitenum’ is a dative past participle agreeing with ‘mē’, ‘to me, having gone forth’, a gentle word for dead. ‘on fæder stǣle’ is ‘in a father’s place’ (‘stǣl’, masculine, ‘place, stead’). At 431–455 Beowulf asked for his mail to go to Higelac if he fell; the request about a father’s place is not recorded there.

sentences.t:
Wes þū mundbora mīnum magoþegnum,
hondgesellum, gif mec hild nime;
sentences.l: Be you a protector to my young-thanes, my hand-companions, if battle take me;
sentences.i: Be a protector to my young thanes, my comrades, if battle takes me;
sentences.n: ‘Wes’ is the imperative of ‘wesan’, and ‘mundbora’ is a ‘protector’ (‘mund’ is the hand as symbol of guardianship, ‘bora’ ‘bearer’, so literally ‘hand-bearer’). ‘mīnum magoþegnum’ and ‘hondgesellum’ are datives, ‘to my young thanes’ and ‘to my hand-companions’, the Geats who have come with him; the apparatus records editors who read ‘hondgesteallum’ or ‘hondgeseldum’ for ‘hondgesellum’, with much the same sense. ‘nime’ is a present subjunctive of ‘niman’, ‘take’: ‘if battle should take me’.

sentences.t:
swylce þū ðā mādmas, þē þū mē sealdest,
Hrōðgār lēofa, Higelāce onsend.
sentences.l: likewise the treasures that you gave me, dear Hrothgar, to Higelac send on.
sentences.i: And send on to Higelac the treasures you gave me, dear Hrothgar.
sentences.n: ‘swylce’ is ‘likewise, also’. ‘ðā mādmas, þē þū mē sealdest’ is an accusative object with a relative clause, ‘the treasures which you gave me’, and ‘onsend’ is the imperative of ‘onsendan’, ‘send on’, with ‘Higelāce’ the dative of the person. The treasures were the gifts Hrothgar gave Beowulf after the fight with Grendel. Sending them to Higelac, Beowulf’s own lord, is how a retainer’s winnings return to his king. Beowulf made the same request at 452, ‘Onsend Higelāce, gif mec hild nime’; there it was the mail, here it is the treasures.

sentences.t:
Mæg þonne on þǣm golde ongitan Gēata dryhten,
gesēon sunu Hrǣdles, þonne hē on þæt sinc starað,
þæt ic gumcystum gōdne funde
bēaga bryttan, brēac þonne mōste.
sentences.l: May the lord of the Geats then perceive on that gold, the son of Hrethel see, when he stares on that treasure, that I found a good giver of rings in manly virtues, and enjoyed him while I might.
sentences.i: Then the lord of the Geats can tell from that gold, and Hrethel’s son can see, as he looks on the treasure, that I found a ring-giver good in manly virtues, and enjoyed his favour while I could.
sentences.n: ‘Mæg’ is a present of ‘magan’, ‘can, may’, and the subject ‘Gēata dryhten’ (‘lord of the Geats’, Higelac) with ‘sunu Hrǣdles’ (‘son of Hrethel’) in apposition. ‘ongitan’ and ‘gesēon’ are the two infinitives, ‘perceive’ and ‘see’, and the ‘þæt’ clause after them says what he will see. ‘Hrǣdles’ is Klaeber’s spelling for the genitive of Hrēðel, Higelac’s father; the apparatus records editors who print ‘Hrēðles’. ‘gumcystum’ is a dative plural, ‘in manly virtues’, with ‘gōdne’ agreeing with ‘bēaga bryttan’, ‘dispenser of rings’ (Hrothgar). ‘brēac’ is the past of ‘brūcan’, ‘enjoy, make use of’, and its object is not stated; I supply ‘him’ and take it as a guess.

sentences.l: And you let Unferth, the widely known man, have the old leaving, the wondrous wave-sword, hard-edged;
sentences.i: And let Unferth, a man known far and wide, have the old heirloom, the wondrous wave-sword with its hard edge;
sentences.n: ‘lǣt’ is the imperative of ‘lǣtan’, ‘let, allow’, with ‘þū’ as its subject, ‘Unferð’ (accusative, not a vocative) as the one allowed and ‘habban’ the infinitive. Klaeber italicises ‘Un’ because the manuscript has ‘hunferð’, and the form ‘Unferð’ is Rieger’s correction. ‘ealde lāfe’ is ‘the old leaving’, an heirloom (‘lāf’, ‘what is left by ancestors’), with ‘wrǣtlīc wǣgsweord’ in apposition. ‘wǣgsweord’ is a compound I read as ‘wave-sword’, a sword with wave-like patterns in the steel; the apparatus lists editors who change it to ‘wīg-’ or ‘wæl-’, which is a guess either way. ‘wīdcūðne man’ is accusative, ‘the widely known man’, Unferth. ‘heardecg’ is ‘hard-edged’. Which sword this is, and whether it is Hrunting itself, the text does not say.

sentences.t:
ic mē mid Hruntinge
dōm gewyrce, oþðe mec dēað nimeð!’
sentences.l: I for myself with Hrunting glory work, or death takes me!’
sentences.i: I shall gain renown for myself with Hrunting, or death will take me!’
sentences.n: ‘ic mē mid Hruntinge dōm gewyrce’ is ‘I with Hrunting work glory for myself’, ‘mē’ dative of advantage, ‘Hruntinge’ the dative of the sword’s name (the house treatment: name left untranslated), and ‘gewyrce’ a first-person present, a form the same in the indicative and the subjunctive, which here gives the force of a resolve. ‘dōm’ is ‘judgement, repute, glory’. ‘oþðe mec dēað nimeð’ is ‘or death takes me’, the indicative ‘nimeð’ stating the alternative flatly. The apparatus notes that the manuscript spells ‘oþðe’ as ‘opðe’, and that a new manuscript leaf (fol. 163a) begins at that word. The closing quotation mark ends Beowulf’s speech.

sentences.l: After those words the Weder-Geats’ man hastened with courage — not at all an answer would he wait for;
sentences.i: After those words the Geat hurried on with courage, and would not wait for any answer;
sentences.n: ‘Æfter þǣm wordum’ is a dative phrase, ‘after those words’, and ‘Weder-Gēata lēod’ ‘the man of the Weder-Geats’ (‘lēod’, ‘man, prince’, Beowulf); ‘Weder’ is a second name for the Geats, and I take it as ‘weather, storm’ without being sure. ‘efste’ is the past of ‘efstan’, ‘hasten’, and ‘mid elne’ ‘with courage’. ‘nalas … bīdan wolde’ is ‘would not at all wait for’, ‘bīdan’ taking ‘andsware’, ‘answer’, which can be read as genitive or accusative (both forms are the same). The dash is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
brimwylm onfēng
hilderince.
sentences.l: the sea-surge received the battle-man.
sentences.i: The surging water of the sea took the warrior in.
sentences.n: ‘brimwylm’ is a compound of ‘brim’, ‘sea’, and ‘wylm’, ‘welling, surge’, here the subject. ‘onfēng’ is the past of ‘onfōn’, ‘receive’, which takes the dative, so ‘hilderince’ (‘hilde’ ‘battle’ plus ‘rinc’ ‘man, warrior’) is the dative object. The sentence has no verb of diving for Beowulf: the sea simply takes him, and his entry into the mere is over in three words.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs hwīl dæges,
ǣr hē þone grundwong ongytan mehte.
sentences.l: Then it was a while of day before he could perceive the ground-plain.
sentences.i: A long part of the day went by before he could make out the bottom of the pool.
sentences.n: ‘Ðā wæs hwīl dæges’ is ‘then was a while of day’, ‘dæges’ a partitive genitive; how long this is the text does not say, and I read ‘a long part of the day’ as a guess. ‘ǣr hē … ongytan mehte’ is ‘before he could perceive’, ‘mehte’ a past subjunctive after ‘ǣr’. ‘grundwong’ is ‘ground-plain’, the floor of the mere pictured as a field.

sentences.t:
Sōna þæt onfunde sē ðe flōda begong
heorogīfre behēold hund missēra,
grim ond grǣdig, þæt þǣr gumena sum
ælwihta eard ufan cunnode.
sentences.l: Soon that perceived she who the circuit of the floods, fierce-greedy, had watched a hundred half-years, grim and greedy, that there a certain one of men the land of strange creatures from above explored.
sentences.i: At once she who had kept watch over the expanse of the waters for a hundred seasons, fierce in greed, grim and ravenous, knew that some human was exploring the creatures’ home from above.
sentences.n: ‘onfunde’ is the past of ‘onfindan’, ‘perceive, find out’, whose subject is the relative clause ‘sē ðe … behēold’, ‘she who watched’. The masculine ‘sē’ is Klaeber’s printed form, though the creature is Grendel’s mother (the feminine ‘sēo’ and ‘hēo’ appear soon after), the same oddity as at 1392. ‘flōda begong’ is ‘the circuit of the floods’. ‘heorogīfre’ is ‘fierce-greedy’; I take ‘heoro-’ as an intensifier, a guess, since it can also mean ‘sword’. ‘hund missēra’ is ‘a hundred half-years’ (‘missēra’ genitive plural), which can be fifty years or a hundred; I do not know. ‘gumena sum’ is ‘a certain one of men’, ‘ælwihta’ ‘of strange creatures’ (‘æl-’ ‘other, foreign’), and ‘ufan’ ‘from above’.

sentences.t:
Grāp þā tōgēanes, gūðrinc gefēng
atolan clommum;
sentences.l: She grasped then toward him, seized the war-man with terrible clamps;
sentences.i: She clutched at him and caught the warrior in her dreadful claws;
sentences.n: The subject ‘she’ is not named; ‘Grāp’ is the past of ‘grīpan’, ‘grasp’, and ‘tōgēanes’ is ‘toward, against’ (him). ‘gūðrinc’ (‘war-man’) is the accusative object of ‘gefēng’, ‘seized’. ‘atolan clommum’ is a dative plural, ‘with terrible clamps’, ‘clom’ (a gripping hold) being the word for her claws or fingers, and ‘atol’ ‘terrible, loathsome’.

sentences.t:
nō þȳ ǣr in gescōd
hālan līce;
sentences.l: none the sooner did she harm in the whole body;
sentences.i: yet she did him no harm for all that, his body stayed whole;
sentences.n: ‘nō þȳ ǣr’ is ‘none the sooner’, ‘þȳ’ an instrumental ‘by that’ with the comparative ‘ǣr’, ‘earlier’. ‘in gescōd’ is the past of ‘gesceþþan’, ‘harm’, with the adverb ‘in’ (‘within’, through the mail), which takes the dative ‘hālan līce’, ‘the sound body’. Beowulf’s armour is the thing that matters in the next lines.

sentences.t:
hring ūtan ymbbearh,
þæt hēo þone fyrdhom ðurhfōn ne mihte,
locene leoðosyrcan lāþan fingrum.
sentences.l: the ring outside protected around, so that she could not pierce through the war-garment, the locked limb-corslet, with her hostile fingers.
sentences.i: The mail on the outside shielded him, so that she could not break through the war-coat, the linked corslet, with those hateful fingers.
sentences.n: ‘hring’ is ‘the ring’, the rings of the mail, subject of ‘ymbbearh’, ‘protected round about’. ‘ūtan’ is ‘from outside’. The ‘þæt’ clause is a result: ‘ne mihte’ ‘could not’, ‘ðurhfōn’ ‘grasp through, pierce’. ‘fyrdhom’ is ‘war-garment’, and ‘locene leoðosyrcan’ is ‘the locked limb-corslet’ (‘leoðu’ ‘limbs’, ‘syrce’ ‘corslet’), ‘locene’ meaning the rings are linked. ‘lāþan fingrum’ is a dative plural, ‘with hateful fingers’. This is the byrnie that Fitt XXI describes before the dive.

sentences.t:
Bær þā sēo brimwyl[f], þā hēo tō botme cōm,
hringa þengel tō hofe sīnum,
sentences.l: Bore then the sea-she-wolf, when she to the bottom came, the prince of rings to her court,
sentences.i: Then the she-wolf of the sea, when she reached the bottom, carried the ring-prince to her hall,
sentences.n: ‘Bær’ is the past of ‘beran’, ‘bear’, and ‘brimwyl[f]’ is the subject: the manuscript has ‘wyl’, and the editor Kemble supplied the ‘f’, hence the square brackets, giving ‘brimwylf’, ‘sea-she-wolf’; the feminine ‘sēo’ and ‘hēo’ support it. ‘hringa þengel’ is ‘prince of rings’ (‘þengel’ ‘prince’, ‘hringa’ genitive plural), a kenning for Beowulf as the giver and owner of rings. ‘tō hofe sīnum’ is ‘to her own court’, ‘hof’ ‘dwelling, hall’ and ‘sīnum’ the reflexive possessive.

sentences.t:
swā hē ne mihte nō — hē þǣm mōdig wæs —
wǣpna gewealdan,
sentences.l: so that he could not at all — he was bold for that — wield weapons,
sentences.i: so that, brave as he was, he could not use his weapons,
sentences.n: A result clause: ‘swā hē ne mihte nō’, with the negative doubled, ‘could not at all’. ‘gewealdan’ takes the genitive, so ‘wǣpna’ is ‘of weapons’. The dash-enclosed ‘hē þǣm mōdig wæs’ is ‘he was bold’, but ‘þǣm’ is disputed: the manuscript has ‘þæm’, and editors read ‘þæs’ (‘for that’), ‘þēah’ (‘though’) or ‘þǣr’ (‘there’); several also move ‘nō’ into the next half-line. In the literal version ‘þǣm’ stays ‘for that’; the idiomatic ‘brave as he was’ takes the concessive sense of the ‘þēah’ reading, a guess. Dragged along the bottom, he could not swing a blade.

sentences.t:
ac hine wundra þæs fela
swe[n]cte on sunde, sǣdēor monig
hildetūxum heresyrcan bræc,
ēhton āglǣcan.
sentences.l: but of wonders so many troubled him in the water, many a sea-beast with battle-tusks broke at his war-corslet, the awesome ones pursued him.
sentences.i: but a great many marvels harried him as he swam; sea-beasts by the score tore with their battle-tusks at his war-shirt, and the fearsome ones hounded him.
sentences.n: ‘ac hine … swe[n]cte’ is ‘but troubled him’, ‘hine’ accusative, ‘wundra þæs fela’ a partitive phrase, ‘so many of wonders’. Klaeber added the ‘n’ in brackets: the manuscript has ‘swecte’, and ‘swencte’ is Kemble’s correction to ‘swencan’, ‘trouble, afflict’. ‘sǣdēor monig’ is ‘many a sea-beast’, ‘hildetūxum’ ‘with battle-tusks’, a dative plural of ‘tūsc’ ‘tusk’, spelled ‘tūx’. ‘bræc’ is literally ‘broke’, but since the mail holds (1548), I take it as ‘broke at, tore at’. ‘ēhton’ is the plural past of ‘ēhtan’, ‘pursue’, and ‘āglǣcan’, a nominative plural, is the house ‘awesome one’ of Grendel at 425 and 433 in the plural.

sentences.t:
Ðā se eorl ongeat,
þæt hē [in] nīðsele nāthwylcum wæs,
þǣr him nǣnig wæter wihte ne sceþede,
nē him for hrōfsele hrīnan ne mehte
fǣrgripe flōdes;
sentences.l: Then the earl perceived that he was in some hostile hall, where no water harmed him in any way, nor could, because of the roof-hall, the sudden grip of the flood touch him;
sentences.i: Then the warrior realised that he was in some hall of enmity, where the water did him no harm, and the sudden grasp of the flood could not touch him beneath its roof;
sentences.n: ‘ongeat’ is the past of ‘ongietan’, ‘perceive’, and the ‘þæt’ clause says what: ‘hē … in nīðsele nāthwylcum wæs’, ‘he was in some hostile hall or other’. The ‘[in]’ is Thorkelin’s addition, and the dative ‘nīðsele’ alone would carry the same sense of place. ‘nāthwylcum’ is the fused phrase ‘ne wāt hwylcum’, ‘I know not which’. ‘nǣnig wæter wihte ne sceþede’ is ‘no water harmed in any whit’, ‘sceþede’ taking the dative ‘him’; the apparatus lists editors who change ‘wæter’. ‘nē … hrīnan ne mehte’ has ‘hrīnan’ with the dative, ‘touch’, and ‘for hrōfsele’ is ‘because of the roof-hall’, the hall’s roof holding off the water. The text does not say whether the hall is a cave or an air-filled chamber; its roof keeps the water off.

sentences.t:
fȳrlēoht geseah,
blācne lēoman beorhte scīnan.
sentences.l: Fire-light he saw, a pale beam brightly shine.
sentences.i: He saw a firelight, a bright beam shining clearly.
sentences.n: ‘fȳrlēoht’ is the compound ‘fire-light’, the object of ‘geseah’ (‘saw’), and ‘blācne lēoman’ an accusative with the infinitive ‘scīnan’, ‘shine’: ‘saw a pale beam shine’. ‘blāc’ means ‘shining, bright’ and also ‘pale’, so the English choice is a guess. The apparatus marks the start of a new manuscript leaf (fol. 163b) at ‘fȳr-’ and gives ‘fyr’ as the spelling in the two Thorkelin transcripts (A and B).

sentences.t:
Ongeat þā se gōda grundwyrgenne,
merewīf mihtig;
sentences.l: Perceived then the good one the ground-accursed one, the mere-woman mighty;
sentences.i: Then the good man saw the accursed creature of the depths, that mighty woman of the mere;
sentences.n: ‘Ongeat’ is the past of ‘ongietan’, ‘perceive’, ‘se gōda’ the weak adjective used as a noun, ‘the good one’, Beowulf. ‘grundwyrgenne’ is an accusative feminine and its meaning is a guess: ‘grund’ ‘bottom’ with ‘wyrgen’, which I connect with ‘wearg’, ‘outlaw, accursed being’, as a feminine form. ‘merewīf’ is ‘mere-woman’ (‘mere’ ‘pool, sea’, ‘wīf’ ‘woman’), a compound that names her as a woman, not a beast, while ‘mihtig’ (‘mighty’) is the adjective.

sentences.t:
mægenrǣs forgeaf
hildebille, hond sweng ne oftēah,
þæt hire on hafelan hringmǣl āgōl
grǣdig gūðlēoð.
sentences.l: he gave a rush of might to the battle-blade, the hand did not withhold the swing, so that on her head the ring-marked blade sang out a greedy war-song.
sentences.i: He put the full rush of his strength into the sword, and his hand did not hold back the stroke, so that the ring-patterned blade sang out on her head, a greedy battle-song.
sentences.n: ‘mægenrǣs forgeaf hildebille’ is ‘gave a rush of might to the battle-blade’ (‘forgeaf’ with the dative ‘hildebille’, ‘battle-bill’, a sword, as in Beowulf’s account of his sea-fight in Fitt VIII). ‘hond sweng ne oftēah’ is ‘the hand did not withhold the swing’, ‘hond’ nominative and ‘sweng’ accusative; Klaeber changes the manuscript’s ‘hord swenge’ and prints the changed letters ‘n’ and ‘g’ in italic, and the apparatus lists several other fixes. ‘hringmǣl’ is ‘ring-marked’, the sword with its patterned blade, the subject of ‘āgōl’, ‘sang out’ (‘āgalan’). ‘gūðlēoð’, ‘war-song’, has the same form in nominative and accusative; I take it as the object of ‘āgōl’, the sound of metal on bone as a song.

sentences.t:
Ðā se gist onfand,
þæt se beadolēoma bītan nolde,
aldre sceþðan, ac sēo ecg geswāc
ðēodne æt þearfe;
sentences.l: Then the guest found that the battle-light would not bite, harm her life, but the edge failed the prince at his need;
sentences.i: Then the stranger found that the shining sword would not bite or harm her life, but that the edge failed the prince in his need;
sentences.n: ‘gist’ is ‘guest, stranger’, Beowulf in the monster’s house. ‘beadolēoma’ is ‘battle-light’, a kenning for the sword, from the gleam of the blade; ‘bītan nolde’ is ‘would not bite’, ‘nolde’ giving the sword a will. ‘aldre sceþðan’ is ‘harm life’ with the dative ‘aldre’. ‘sēo ecg geswāc ðēodne’ is ‘the edge failed the prince’, ‘geswāc’ the past of ‘geswīcan’ with the dative. ‘æt þearfe’ is ‘at need’, the same phrase as at 1477. Hrunting, lent by Unferth, is the sword that fails.

sentences.l: it had endured before many hand-meetings, often sheared a helm, a doomed man’s war-garment;
sentences.i: Before this it had come through many hand-to-hand fights and often cut through a helmet and the war-coat of a doomed man;
sentences.n: ‘ðolode’ is the past of ‘ðolian’, ‘endure, undergo’, with ‘fela hondgemōta’, ‘many hand-meetings’ (partitive genitive plural), the fights at close quarters. ‘gescær’ is the past of ‘gescieran’, ‘cut through’, ‘helm’ and ‘fyrdhrægl’ (‘army-garment’, mail) its two objects, set side by side with no ‘and’. ‘fǣges’ is the genitive of ‘fǣge’, ‘doomed to die’, a word of the poem’s fate-language: the sword’s old victims were already marked for death.

sentences.t:
ðā wæs forma sīð
dēorum mādme, þæt his dōm ālæg.
sentences.l: then was for the first time for the precious treasure, that its glory lay down.
sentences.i: This was the first time that the precious blade’s renown failed it.
sentences.n: ‘ðā wæs forma sīð’ is ‘then was the first time’, ‘dēorum mādme’ a dative, ‘for the dear treasure’, the sword, and ‘mādm’ ‘treasure’ is the word for a thing of value. ‘his dōm ālæg’ is ‘its glory lay low’: ‘ālæg’ is the past of ‘ālicgan’, ‘lie down, fail’, and ‘his’ is the neuter possessive, ‘its’. ‘dōm’ is the word of Beowulf’s vow at 1491. Fitt XXI said at 1460 that the sword never failed its bearer.

sentences.t:
Eft wæs anrǣd, nalas elnes læt,
mǣrða gemyndig mǣg Hȳlāces:
sentences.l: Again he was firm of purpose, not at all slack in courage, mindful of glories, the kinsman of Higelac:
sentences.i: Once more he was resolute, no whit slow in valour, mindful of glory, Higelac’s kinsman:
sentences.n: ‘anrǣd’ is ‘single-counselled, resolute’; ‘læt’ is ‘slow’ and takes the genitive ‘elnes’, so ‘nalas elnes læt’ is ‘not at all slack in courage’, and ‘mǣrða gemyndig’ is ‘mindful of glories’, with ‘gemyndig’ taking the genitive. ‘mǣg Hȳlāces’ is ‘kinsman of Higelac’; Klaeber prints ‘Hȳlāces’ where the manuscript has ‘hylaces’, and the apparatus lists the other readings (‘Hygelāces’, ‘Hyglāces’), all the same name. Beowulf is Higelac’s nephew. The colon introduces what he does next.

sentences.t:
wearp ðā wundenmǣl wrǣttum gebunden
yrre ōretta, þæt hit on eorðan læg,
stīð ond stȳlecg; strenge getrūwọde,
mundgripe mægenes.
sentences.l: threw then the twist-patterned blade, bound with ornaments, angry the fighter, so that it lay on the earth, stiff and steel-edged; in strength he trusted, in the hand-grip of might.
sentences.i: The angry champion flung down the patterned sword, bound with ornaments, so that it lay on the ground, stiff and steel-edged; he trusted to his strength, the hand-grip of his might.
sentences.n: ‘wearp’ is the past of ‘weorpan’, ‘throw’, ‘wundenmǣl’ (‘twist-patterned’, ‘wunden’ being ‘twisted’, as in ‘wundenfeax’ at 1400; a wavy pattern or twisted inlay) its object. The manuscript has ‘wundel’, Kemble read ‘wunden-’, and Klaeber prints the changed ‘n’ in italic. ‘wrǣttum gebunden’ is ‘bound with ornaments’, ‘yrre ōretta’ ‘angry fighter’. ‘stīð ond stȳlecg’ describes the lying sword, ‘stiff’ and ‘steel-edged’; the apparatus sends the reader to the variants at 669b. ‘strenge getrūwọde’ is ‘trusted in strength’, ‘getrūwọde’ the past of ‘getrūwian’ with the dative. The dot under the ‘ọ’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. ‘mundgripe mægenes’ is ‘in the hand-grip of might’.

sentences.t:
Swā sceal man dôn,
þonne hē æt gūðe gegān þenceð
longsumne lof; nā ymb his līf cearað.
sentences.l: So shall a man do, when he thinks in battle to gain long-lasting praise; he does not care about his life.
sentences.i: So a man must act when he means to win lasting fame in battle; he does not worry about his life.
sentences.n: ‘sceal’ is ‘must, shall’, and ‘dôn’ is the infinitive of ‘dōn’, ‘do’; the circumflex in ‘dôn’ is Klaeber’s mark for a contracted vowel. ‘þonne hē … þenceð’ is ‘when he intends’, ‘gegān’ ‘obtain, gain’, ‘longsumne lof’ ‘lasting praise’. The semicolon divides the rule from the application: ‘nā ymb his līf cearað’ is ‘he does not care about his life’, ‘cearað’ present of ‘cearian’, ‘be anxious’, with ‘ymb’. The maxim comments on the thrown sword: Beowulf stakes the fight on his own strength.

sentences.t:
Gefēng þā be eaxle — nalas for fǣhðe mearn —
Gūð-Gēata lēod Grendles mōdor;
sentences.l: He seized then by the shoulder — not at all for the feud did he mourn — the war-Geats’ man, Grendel’s mother;
sentences.i: Then the Geat seized Grendel’s mother by the shoulder, and had no anxiety over the feud;
sentences.n: The sentence is in a loose order: ‘Gefēng … Grendles mōdor’ is ‘seized Grendel’s mother’, with the subject ‘Gūð-Gēata lēod’, ‘the man of the War-Geats’, inserted between. ‘be eaxle’ is ‘by the shoulder’; the apparatus lists editors who read ‘feaxe’, ‘hair’, but Klaeber keeps ‘eaxle’. ‘nalas for fǣhðe mearn’ is ‘did not at all grieve for the feud’, ‘mearn’ the past of ‘murnan’: he did not fear the quarrel that would follow. The dashes are Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
brægd þā beadwe heard, þā hē gebolgen wæs,
feorhgenīðlan, þæt hēo on flet gebēah.
sentences.l: he swung her then, hard in battle, when he was enraged, the life-enemy, so that she bowed to the floor.
sentences.i: Hard in battle and filled with rage, he flung the deadly foe so that she dropped to the floor.
sentences.n: ‘brægd’ is the past of ‘bregdan’, ‘pull, swing’; the object is ‘feorhgenīðlan’, ‘life-enemy’ (‘feorh’ ‘life’ and ‘genīðla’ ‘enemy’), a weak accusative. ‘beadwe heard’ is ‘hard in battle’, ‘beadwe’ dative of ‘beadu’, and ‘gebolgen’ is ‘enraged’, a participle. ‘flet’ is ‘floor’ (the word also names the floor of a hall) and ‘gebēah’ the past of ‘gebūgan’, ‘bend, sink down’.

sentences.t:
Hēo him eft hraþe andlēan forgeald
grimman grāpum ond him tōgēanes fēng;
sentences.l: She repaid him again quickly with a requital, with grim grasps, and seized toward him;
sentences.i: She repaid him quickly in turn with her fierce grip and clutched at him;
sentences.n: ‘Hēo him eft hraþe andlēan forgeald’ is ‘she to him in turn quickly repaid requital’; ‘forgeald’ is the past of ‘forgieldan’, ‘repay’. The manuscript has ‘handlean’, and Klaeber’s ‘andlēan’ (the changed ‘a’ is italic) is Rieger’s correction; ‘andlēan’ is ‘requital’. ‘grimman grāpum’ is ‘with grim grasps’, ‘grimman’ standing for the dative plural ‘grimmum’, and ‘fēng’ the past of ‘fōn’, ‘seize’, with ‘tōgēanes’ and the dative ‘him’. The apparatus notes that a new manuscript leaf (fol. 164a) begins in the middle of ‘grimman’.

sentences.t:
oferwearp þā wērigmōd wigena strengest,
fēþecempa, þæt hē on fylle wearð.
sentences.l: overthrew then, weary-minded, the strongest of warriors, the foot-fighter, so that he came to a fall.
sentences.i: The strongest of warriors, weary at heart, a fighter on foot, stumbled, and fell.
sentences.n: A hard sentence. ‘oferwearp’ is the past of ‘oferweorpan’, ‘throw over’, and has no object in the text; the nominative ‘wērigmōd wigena strengest, fēþecempa’ (‘weary-minded, strongest of warriors, foot-fighter’) can only be Beowulf. I read the verb as ‘overthrew himself’, ‘stumbled’, so that ‘hē’ in the next clause is also Beowulf, and the next lines show him on his back. Two editors supply ‘[hine]’ in the apparatus, ‘overthrew him’; that is a guess either way. ‘on fylle wearð’ is ‘came to a fall’ (‘wearð’ past of ‘weorðan’, ‘become’). ‘fēþecempa’ is ‘foot-fighter’, one who fights on foot; the apparatus lists editors who change the case endings.

sentences.t:
Ofsæt þā þone selegyst, ond hyre seax getēah
brād [ond] brūnecg; wolde hire bearn wrecan,
āngan eaferan.
sentences.l: She sat on the hall-guest, and drew her knife, broad and brown-edged; she would avenge her child, her only offspring.
sentences.i: She sat upon the stranger and drew her broad knife with its dark edge, meaning to avenge her son, her only child.
sentences.n: ‘Ofsæt’ is the past of ‘ofsittan’, ‘sit upon’. ‘selegyst’ is ‘hall-guest’ (‘sele’ ‘hall’, ‘gyst’ ‘guest’), Beowulf in her hall. ‘seax’ is a knife; the manuscript has ‘seaxe’, and Klaeber’s ‘seax’ has the changed ‘x’ in italic. ‘brād [ond] brūnecg’ is ‘broad and brown-edged’, with ‘ond’ in brackets because Grundtvig added it; ‘brūnecg’ may mean ‘burnished’, which is a guess. ‘wolde’ is ‘she meant to’, ‘bearn’ ‘child’ the object, and ‘āngan eaferan’ ‘only offspring’ in apposition. Her motive is a mother’s vengeance, as at 1276 (‘sunu dēoð wrecan’) and 1339 (‘wolde hyre mǣg wrecan’).

sentences.t:
Him on eaxle læg
brēostnet brōden; þæt gebearh fēore,
wið ord ond wið ecge ingang forstōd.
sentences.l: On his shoulder lay the braided breast-net; that protected his life, against point and against edge it withstood entry.
sentences.i: On his shoulder lay the woven mail; it saved his life and kept out the point and the edge.
sentences.n: ‘brēostnet’ is ‘breast-net’, mail-shirt, ‘brōden’ ‘braided’ (the past participle of ‘bregdan’). ‘gebearh’ is the past of ‘gebeorgan’, ‘protect’, taking the dative ‘fēore’, ‘life’. ‘wið ord ond wið ecge’ is ‘against point and against edge’, ‘ingang’ the accusative ‘entrance’, and ‘forstōd’ ‘withstood, stood in the way of’. The mail that stopped her fingers a few lines ago now stops her knife.

sentences.t:
Hæfde ðā forsīðod sunu Ecgþēowes
under gynne grund, Gēata cempa,
nemne him heaðobyrne helpe gefremede,
herenet hearde,
sentences.l: Would then have perished the son of Ecgtheow under the wide ground, the Geats’ champion, if the battle-byrnie had not afforded him help, the hard war-net,
sentences.i: The son of Ecgtheow, the Geats’ champion, would then have perished under the wide earth, had his battle-corslet not given him help, that strong war-net,
sentences.n: ‘Hæfde … forsīðod’ is ‘had perished’, a pluperfect that here means ‘would have perished’; ‘forsīðod’ is the past participle of ‘forsīðian’, ‘come to ruin on the way’. ‘gynne grund’ is ‘wide ground’, the floor of the mere. ‘nemne him … gefremede’ is ‘unless it had done help for him’, ‘nemne’ ‘unless’ with the past subjunctive. ‘heaðobyrne’ is ‘battle-byrnie’ (‘heaðo’ ‘battle’), and ‘herenet’ ‘war-net’, a second kenning for the mail, as at 1548.

sentences.t:
— ond hālig God
gewēold wīgsigor;
sentences.l: — and holy God ruled war-victory;
sentences.i: and holy God ruled the victory in the war;
sentences.n: ‘ond hālig God gewēold wīgsigor’ is ‘and holy God controlled victory in war’; ‘gewēold’ is the past of ‘gewealdan’, ‘rule, control’, and ‘wīgsigor’ ‘war-victory’. The dash before it is Klaeber’s, as printed in ‘t’. The narrator steps in here to say, in Christian terms, whose hand decided the fight.

sentences.t:
wītig Drihten,
rodera Rǣdend hit on ryht gescēd
ȳðelīce, syþðan hē eft āstōd.
sentences.l: the wise Lord, Ruler of the heavens, decided it rightly, easily, after he stood up again.
sentences.i: The wise Lord, Ruler of the heavens, settled it justly and without trouble once Beowulf had risen to his feet.
sentences.n: ‘wītig Drihten’ and ‘rodera Rǣdend’ are two titles in apposition, ‘wise Lord’ and ‘Ruler of the heavens’ (‘rodera’ genitive plural of ‘rodor’, ‘sky, heaven’), the subject of ‘gescēd’, ‘decided’ (‘gescēadan’). ‘on ryht’ is ‘in right, rightly’. ‘ȳðelīce’ is ‘easily’. ‘syþðan hē eft āstōd’ is ‘after he stood up again’, the subject ‘hē’ Beowulf, and ‘āstōd’ the past of ‘āstandan’. The fitt ends on Beowulf upright.
